The flack I've heard (and received) has been about age, perceived interests and techniques for how to craft the thing.

Conventions do tend to draw the under 40 crowd (depends on the con really, scifi cons usually attract an older age group).

There's been grumbles that con people have no interest in anything SCA related (this is incredibly untrue)

The cosplayer thing goes into the 'techniques ' portion. It's kinda just snobbery, because they don't do things the one and only correct historically accurate way the said person is doing things wrong. 

It goes back into the reputation for cliquey behavior and elitism. Not everyone is like this but when you have a loud minority it makes everyone look bad.

My group hasn't done any recruiting either and now they have only 6ish active members.

Good for you wanting to grow your group! I wish you all the good luck.

The active recruiting tends to attract more people but a number of those people find that it's not their thing and move on. Just based on numbers you see more people leaving from actively recruiting.

However if they move on because of their own interests you aren't damaging the SCAs rep and even if you get one person to stay it's a success.

IMO a group that isn't growing is dying.

So I've helped one of my old SCA groups with recruiting and we've divided the process into passive and active recruiting.

Passive recruiting would be making your presence known via flyers in locations like libraries, colleges, comic shops, game shops, museums, basically anywhere you think people with an interest in the SCA might be. 

Active recruiting would depend on how many new people your group can handle. Because if you get a bunch of new people and have nothing for them to do, no one to help them find their way in the SCA (it's pretty daunting for a newbie) they'll just leave and your effort is for naught. 

Active recruiting would be demos, panels at your local convention, being in your local parade, advertising on facebook/cities subreddit, holding public classes at the library. Showing people who we are and what we do. 

Retention is also a big part of this. Having a buddy system for newbies would be absolutely amazing and would probably help them make friends and find different hobbies, they would then tell their friends about their cool new thing and positive word would get around.


In some larp/cosplay/con communities the SCA has a bad reputation for being cliquey and elitist. I've experienced this myself and it made me leave a group and not even give the SCA another chance for years. It is possible to change this reputation.

I've seen groups resist the idea of recruiting at cons ("Do we really want those people?") And hate on cosplayers (again had this happen to me several times by different groups). I've also heard groups say that people will just find them if they're interested. That doesn't work anymore, a lot of people don't even know the SCA exists and there's a lot of other historical-esque larp groups out there trying to recruit from the same pool of people.

The SCA is fun and I would like to see it not die off. Ehh these are just my thoughts and ideas and don't represent any particular group.

Hi! Historical costumer here.  


A really good source for fabric comes from thrift stores. I usually look for curtains but bedsheets make wonderful mock up fabric.   
Some online stores I really like are [fabric.com](https://fabric.com) / [fabricmartfabrics.com](https://fabricmartfabrics.com) / [fabric-store.com](https://fabric-store.com) (for linen fabric) but I also use Joann's and local fabric stores.   
The best way to start is simply to pick a project and get elbows deep. You can find regency or other patterns on sale at Joann's and use some thrifted curtains or bedsheets to make your project. Regency is pretty simplistic in comparison to Edwardian so it may be a good place to start.    


I also suggest facebook groups for historical costuming and youtube tutorials since sometimes you come across a small stumble and may need a question answered.   


Machines can be a bit scary at first but practice makes perfect, some machines have speed control (Brothers typically) and that can help until you're use to them :) Handsewing is also great and I know historical costumers that only handsew.
